idiom_name: contiguous homogeneous storage + handles, with hot/cold splitting and a packed active prefix
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: replace the object graph with storage shaped like the loop. Keep one contiguous array (or one array per field) per record type, store records by value, and reference them through handles (indices or ids) rather than pointers, so growth, sorting and packing cannot dangle. Iterate a count of active elements instead of testing a flag per element, and keep the active ones at the front with swap-based activation/deactivation. Once access patterns are known, split each record into the fields touched every iteration and the rarely used tail, keeping the hot part packed and the cold part behind a single pointer or a parallel array at the same index. Only do this where a profiler shows cache misses dominate, and keep a thin facade (handles/views) at the boundary so callers need not know the internal layout.
code_sketch:
records = packed array of T           # one allocation, values not pointers
handles = indices into records       # stable across growth and reordering
loop over 0..active_count:
    records[i].update(dt)            # no chase, no flag test
activate(h):   records[active_count], records[h] = records[h], records[active_count]; active_count += 1
deactivate(h): active_count -= 1; records[h] = records[active_count]
# hot/cold split:
#   struct Hot  { x, y, vx, vy }             # touched every frame, packed
#   struct Cold { loot, dialogue, history }  # one pointer away, touched rarely
# SoA variant:
#   xs = array of float; ys = array of float; vxs = array of float; vys = array of float
#   loop over i: xs[i] += vxs[i] * dt  # unit stride, SIMD-friendly
pitfalls: Keeping pointers or references into the storage recreates the dangling-reference problem the pattern removes; hand out handles and resolve them per access.
Packing by sorting every frame costs more than the cache misses it prevents; maintain the active prefix incrementally at activation/deactivation instead.
Reshaping every data structure 'because cache' without a profile produces rigid code, longer build times and no measurable win.

In SoA, forgetting to keep parallel arrays in sync during insert/delete/swap: a mistaken index in one column corrupts the record across all fields — use a typed wrapper that atomically performs operations across all arrays.

Aligning to cache-line boundaries (64 bytes) for hot records shared between threads, but forgetting padding at the end of a struct that sits in an array — the array layout then misaligns every other element.

Wrong move: adopting SoA/ECS as a universal default because 'data-oriented' names the pattern -> the layout adds column bookkeeping and TLB pressure with no measured cache win on workloads that read whole records anyway -> instead profile first and let the dominant access pattern (single-field sweep vs whole-record access) pick the layout.

Wrong move: splitting every multi-field record into one array per field -> loops that read x, y, z together now fault in three cache lines per element instead of one, losing the locality AoS already provided -> instead keep fields consumed together in one struct and extract only the fields that are processed alone across many records.

Wrong move: assuming 'packed' means one fully contiguous allocation and caching a raw pointer to the whole pool -> paged or chunked stores (EnTT pages, Unity archetype chunks) break contiguity at page boundaries and the raw walk runs off the span -> instead iterate page by page or use the library's raw/chunk APIs, and verify contiguity before any pointer fast path.
